definition: Validate means to confirm that something is accurate, sound, or officially acceptable — to put it through a check it must pass.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word validate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know validate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Crash tests validated the redesigned bumper months before the first car left the line.
Support is weaker than validate: evidence that supports a method just leans its way, while validating the method means it has actually passed the checks that could have sunk it.
Certify goes further than validate — a validated result has passed its test, but a certified one carries an authority's official seal, with the confirmation itself written into a document.

To confirm is to establish that something is true — a fact, a booking, a rumor. Validate is narrower and more procedural: you confirm a fact, but you validate a thing against a test or a standard — a method, a ticket, a result.
To endorse is to declare public support — a vote of confidence from a person. Validation is a demonstration, not a vote: the thing itself passes a check, whoever happens to be cheering for it.
to show that a claim or method is false
to prove an argument or claim wrong

Validate means to confirm that something is accurate, sound, or officially acceptable — to put it through a check it must pass.
When the marathon winner beat the state record by forty seconds, nobody doubted the clock — they doubted the course.

Officials spent the next week validating it: re-riding the route with calibrated measuring wheels and checking every turn against the certified map, and only when the course itself had passed inspection did the record stand.
Validate fits because what gets confirmed is soundness against a standard: the course must measure what a marathon must measure, and the checking is the whole point.
Corroborate would need a second witness telling the same story; authenticate, taught earlier in this unit, would ask whether the course was genuine rather than whether it held up.
Validation is the passed test.
Validate is the workhorse of labs, registrars, and parking garages: something is checked against a standard and passes — data, tickets, credentials, results.
Don't reach for it when you mean corroborate, this unit's second-source verb: validation needs a test, not another witness.
And its softer modern use — validating someone's feelings — is real English, but in analytical writing keep the word for checks that something could fail.

The forecasting team had used the same avalanche model for a decade, but the new terrain scanner promised sharper predictions.
Promise was not enough for the safety board: before any ranger could rely on the scanner, the team had to validate it.
All spring they ran the device against slopes whose stability was already known, checking its output against a hundred past slides.
Twice the scanner failed the margin the board required, and twice the engineers went back to the workbench.
In June it finally passed every check on the list, and only then did its readings start appearing in the morning bulletins.
